docs.text:
Welcome to DSAA3073 - Theories in Data Science!

This course provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for data science, covering statistical learning theory, computational learning theory, optimization, and online learning algorithms.

docs.title: 🎯 Course Overview
docs.text: This course covers fundamental theories that underpin modern data science and machine learning:

docs.title: Course Structure (13 Lectures, 9 Weeks of Content)
docs.text:
Phase 1: Foundations (Lectures 1-5) - Week 1: Mathematical Preliminaries (probability, linear algebra, optimization) - Weeks 2-3: PAC Learning Framework, VC Dimension, Uniform Convergence, Fundamental Theorem

Phase 2: Classical Methods (Lectures 6-8) - Week 4: Bias-Variance Tradeoff & Regularization - Week 5: Cross-Validation & Model Selection Criteria

Phase 3: Ensemble Learning (Lectures 9-10) - Weeks 6-7: Boosting Theory (AdaBoost, Margin Theory, Loss Minimization)

Phase 4: Online Learning (Lectures 11-13) - Weeks 8-9: Expert Advice, Regret Analysis, Online Convex Optimization

Note: Deep learning theory (Weeks 10-12) is not included in the 13-week lecture structure.

docs.title: Session Format
docs.text:
• 30-minute validation test (assessing previous lecture's material)
  • 10-minute break
  • ~130 minutes of self-paced learning with instructor support
  • Voluntary tutorials in the evening for group-based learning

docs.title: How to Succeed
docs.text:
1. Follow the lecture mapping - Each lecture covers specific sections of weekly learning sheets
  2. Work through learning sheets systematically - Follow the narrative flow
  3. Use validation sheets to test your understanding
  4. Ask questions during class - Instructor circulates to provide guidance
  5. Attend tutorials for collaborative problem-solving

docs.title: 🎓 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  1. Understand theoretical foundations of statistical and computational learning
  2. Analyze generalization guarantees and sample complexity of learning algorithms
  3. Apply PAC learning framework, VC dimension, and Rademacher complexity
  4. Design and analyze regularization and model selection techniques
  5. Prove convergence guarantees for boosting and online learning algorithms
  6. Bridge theory and practice in modern machine learning applications

docs.title: 💡 Prerequisites
docs.text:
This course assumes:

  • ✅ Strong foundation in linear algebra, calculus, and probability
  • ✅ Familiarity with basic algorithms and data structures
  • ✅ Comfort with mathematical proofs and formal reasoning
  • ✅ Programming experience for implementing theoretical concepts

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
You are free to choose a written assignment or a programming project for this course. The assignment/project should be closely related to the topics covered in the course. You must obtain approval from the instructor before starting your work. The assignment/project should be completed individually, and you are expected to submit your work by the mid of the exam period of this semester.

Some ideas for the assignment/project include:

  • Implementing a specific algorithm or data structure discussed in the course, then analyzing its performance and possible improvements.
  • Conducting a small research project on a topic related to the course, such as exploring a new problem from a theoretical aspect (for example, a model or a hypothesis).
  • Possible topics:
    • Investigate how an LLM generalizes in the OOD case.
    • Explore alternative theoretical models to explain the generalization and PEFT of foundation models.
    • Explore Grokking and its theoretical foundations.

Last updated: June 14, 2026

docs.title: Grade Descriptors
docs.text: Grade Performance Level Description A Excellent Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of statistical learning theory, PAC learning, and optimization. Can construct rigorous proofs, apply generalization bounds fluently, and synthesize concepts across topics. Shows creativity in problem-solving. B Good Shows solid understanding of core concepts and can correctly apply techniques for most problems. Proofs are generally correct with minor gaps. Can identify appropriate approaches for standard problems. C Satisfactory Demonstrates adequate knowledge of fundamental definitions and theorems. Can solve routine problems but struggles with novel applications or complex proofs. D Marginal Pass Shows threshold understanding of basic concepts but has difficulty with proofs and theoretical analysis. Can recognize problems but struggles to solve them independently. F Fail Demonstrates insufficient understanding of core concepts. Unable to construct valid proofs or apply basic techniques. Does not meet minimum requirements.
